A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Demon research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation experiments, reward-estimation analyses, VLM and manual-selection demonstrations, and a 101-participant study in Appendix F.2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports revised comparisons, a redesigned VLM experiment, and additional HPDv2 evaluation in Appendix F.

M1.justification: The core Tanh/Boltzmann algorithms, Heun stepping and noise projection are retained. The VLM adaptation changes: v1 compares each candidate against the current state's reconstruction and assigns ±0.5; v2 applies two Quicksort partitions among 16 candidates and assigns +1 to roughly the best eight and −1 to the rest.

E1.justification: New Appendix F evaluates 10 prompts sampled from HPDv2, extending the evaluated prompt corpus beyond the existing animal and custom-prompt experiments. Text-to-image preference alignment remains the task, and HPSv2 itself was already used as a reward and metric in v1.

E2.justification: Table 3 substantially broadens its comparison set by adding DPO, Universal Guidance (Uni, CLIP-guided), and Best-of-N; Table 4 adds their qualitative outputs. DPO and Best-of-N already appeared elsewhere in v1 but are new to this comparison. Figure 4 also adds consistency-model and consistency-model Best-of-N references.

E3.justification: The animal comparison changes from 22 to 45 prompts, the reported SD v1.4 baseline to SD v1.5, and beta from 0.1 to 0.5. Table 2 replaces RMSE with error standard deviation, six-step with four-step ODE estimation, and 40-step with 200-step state preparation. VLM experiments change APIs, prompts and sampling settings. DOODL's reported aesthetics optimization budget changes from 50 to 25 iterations.

E4.justification: Table 2 revises the reward-estimator accuracy-versus-cost analysis, testing four-step instead of six-step ODE estimation and five instead of three noise levels. The temperature, K and beta ablations in Appendix B, PickScore trajectory analysis, and human-study analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The reported Monte Carlo sample count for estimating the reference reward changes from 100 in v1's Section 5 to 200 in v2's Appendix I.5. This changes the statistical estimation procedure. Standard-deviation bands and mean-plus/minus reporting already appear in v1 and are retained.

E6.justification: Figure 4 and Table 2 report revised results under changed settings, and Appendix F adds HPDv2 outcomes. Table 3 retains its original scores while adding comparator results, including Best-of-N's aesthetics score of 6.32 ± 0.34. The VLM finding changes from 14 of 16 improved images to all eight revised outputs exceeding PF-ODE on relative PickScore probabilities; these are different experiments, not a same-setting gain.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 corrects the factor of two in the Itô correction term, and Lemma 3 replaces boundedness of the reward estimate with an L-Lipschitz assumption. Lemma 2 explicitly assumes equality of the reward estimators and references the sample-centered Equation (10), whereas v1's statement specified weights centered on r_beta(x_t). These are localized revisions to the formal assumptions and reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: inference-time alignment without training or backpropagation, compatibility with non-differentiable rewards, plug-and-play integration, theoretical reward improvement, and improved aesthetics scores. The additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 attributes resistance to reward hacking to the absence of backpropagation, replacing v1's statement that the underlying reason was unclear. It also replaces caution about whether optimized scores demonstrate perceptual preferences with more affirmative interpretations and adds an Ensemble-versus-Best-of-N interpretation. The near-harmonic reward assumption and runtime/accuracy limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and newly discloses that DOODL used an RTX A6000 while other experiments used an RTX 3090, including a reported relative speed of 0.92x. Appendix I.5 also specifies 200 SDE steps per reference Monte Carlo sample and the VLM stopping point at t = 8. These extend the existing implementation documentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Yoon et al. (2023) to the alignment literature and Hoare (1962) for Quicksort, while removing the Radford et al. (2021) reference accompanying the old VLM evaluation discussion. The broader positioning and novelty claim remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Parts of Sections 4–5 are rewritten and appendix proofs are condensed. Computational considerations become Section 4.3, Tanh/Boltzmann subsections become paragraph headings, and appendices are reorganized around the new HPDv2 section. Publication headers and acknowledgements change, while the overall narrative and section sequence remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Several central displays are substantially revised: Figure 4 is redrawn, Table 2 expands, Table 3 gains comparator rows and timing, and Tables 4–5 are redesigned. New Figure 9 and Table 11 display HPDv2 results; v1's four VLM score matrices are removed in favor of the new Table 5 display. The original Table 4 reward gallery is retained in v2's Tables 14–15.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons in Table 3 and the HPDv2 benchmark strengthen empirical validation, while code/hardware disclosures and the Itô/Lipschitz corrections improve verifiability. These gains are partly offset by less qualified reward-hacking and perceptual interpretations, and by Table 2 replacing bias-sensitive RMSE with error standard deviation. The evidence supports a limited net improvement, without establishing direct performance gains across the changed settings.
